note: Said 'key'. Taíno by way of Spanish cayo; the buccaneers brought it into English for 'small insular spots with a scant vegetation' (Smyth). The usual word on these charts
Older spelling of cay, recorded from 1693; use now and then for variety, never in the same world as Cay for the same specific
Norse and British: 'a small uninhabited island used for pasture' (Smyth). Grassy, northern-sounding
Plain English for the smallest islands
The storybook word; small to middling islands
A single rock, awash or standing
Old Norse sker: an isolated rock in the sea
A pillar standing off the shore; only for islands with a stack
Norse and Hebridean: an islet off a larger island, as a calf beside a cow, like the Calf of Man. Takes the name of its neighbour
Spanish, for the older layer of names; use sparingly with Spanish specifics
French Antilles, as above with French specifics
